title: AMD attacks Nvidia's FP64 emulation at SC26, touts native double-precision on Instinct MI430X
summary: AMD is touting the benefits of the native FP64 support provided by its MI430X accelerator at Supercomputing 2026. The company says that Ozaki FP64 emulation only covers the needs of a small portion of HPC workloads, making the MI430X a unique foundation for next-gen supercomputing installations.
body: As Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) opens in Chicago this week, AMD is indirectly needling Nvidia about the lack of native FP64 data type support in its data center GPU products. FP64, or double-precision floating-point math, is widely used in the high-performance scientific computing and simulation fields that are the focus of SC26. For those customers, AMD is trumpeting the value of its latest Instinct MI430X accelerator for customers that still need native FP64, like national laboratories and supercomputing centers. Over the past few years, Nvidia has reallocated die area on its data center GPUs to favor the lower-precision matrix math that boosts the operations needed for much of modern AI inference. That reallocation only makes business sense, as the total addressable market for AI compute has exploded while the demand for double-precision math in large supercomputing installations has remained flat by comparison. To make up for the lack of native FP64 support, Nvidia has turned to techniques that allow it to emulate FP64 operations using methods like the Ozaki schemes. But AMD claims this kind of emulation is nowhere close to a replacement for native double-precision processing fo…

title: Nvidia announces Rubin HPC GPU with 'record number of CUDA cores' at Supercomputing 2026
summary: Nvidia took the wraps off its Rubin HPC GPU at Supercomputing 2026. This new GPU will give scientists, engineers, and analysts over 50,000 CUDA cores to speed up agentic HPC workloads when it arrives in 2028.
body: The Supercomputing 2026 conference is under way, and despite continuing turmoil elsewhere in the company, Nvidia has lots to reveal at the show. Foremost among its announcements today, Nvidia took the wraps off a new member of the Rubin GPU family called Rubin HPC , a chip that the company says is meant to accelerate agentic workflows and simulation for scientists, engineers, and analysts working with large data sets. To accelerate those most demanding workloads, Nvidia says Rubin HPC has the highest number of CUDA cores on any of its GPUs - "more than 50,000" - which might imply that this chip uses a configuration similar to the four-die Rubin Ultra GPU, which links those dies together using NVLink-C2C. Today's Rubin GPU has 224 SMs and 28,672 CUDA cores, so scaling compute resources to the degree Rubin HPC does would necessarily require more dies on a package. Nvidia didn't reveal more details of the chip's physical layout alongside the announcement. (The representative image shared by the company wouldn't appear to take this into account.) To keep data moving between Rubin HPC GPUs, Nvidia will use its NVLink 7 interconnect. The company didn't share any new details of the bandw…

title: Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files
summary: Aaron Christophel ported Doom to the LCD on a MOVESPEED MSSU10 flash drive and controls it with file transfers.
body: Doom now runs on a USB flash drive ’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video . The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen. The off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally shows status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature. title: Cockpit-Simulator 737X CDU (v2) Review: An Essential Component for Flight Sim Enthusiasts
summary: The CS 737X CDU (v2) by Cockpit-Simulator is a plug-and-play, 1:1 replica of a Boeing 737 Control Display Unit for home cockpit builds.
body: Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits. Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment. Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024. The Real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality. The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS).
